analysis.investment_thesis: H.G. Infra is a capital-hungry EPC contractor with no discernible moat, consistently negative free cash flow for all five years examined, and a debt load that nearly quadrupled in a single year (borrowings: INR 1,513 Cr → INR 5,669 Cr in FY25). While optically cheap at 10.6x P/E, the business destroys cash at an accelerating rate and competes purely on bid pricing — the antithesis of a wonderful company.
key_strengths: Strong historical earnings CAGR of 36.8% over 9 years (2016–2025), demonstrating execution capability
Decent operating margins of 18.6% for an EPC contractor, above sector peers
High promoter holding at 71.78% signals founder-level commitment to the business
key_risks: Catastrophic free cash flow: FCF was -INR 2,415 Cr in FY25 alone; negative in all 5 of 5 years — this business consumes cash relentlessly
Debt explosion: borrowings surged 274% in one year (1,513 → 5,669 Cr); finance costs growing at 36.6% CAGR, faster than revenue
No economic moat: EPC contracts are won on price bids, not brand or switching costs — competitors can replicate every capability
red_flags: Operating cash flow negative in 4 of last 5 years — reported profits are largely accounting profits, not cash
CWIP surged from INR 14 Cr to INR 1,322 Cr in FY25, suggesting massive speculative capital deployment
Revenue and net profit both declined in FY25 (revenue -6%, net profit -6%) despite massive new debt
Finance costs of INR 265 Cr now consuming ~52% of net profit, up from INR 16 Cr in 2016
analysis.detailed_analysis:
H.G. Infra is precisely the type of business I have spent a career avoiding: capital-intensive, competitively undifferentiated, and dependent on government contract flows. EPC contractors win work by underbidding rivals — there is no brand loyalty, no switching cost, no network effect. The moment NHAI slows project awards or a competitor prices lower, the order book evaporates. The 9-year revenue CAGR of 23.8% is impressive on the surface, but it has been fueled entirely by external capital. The company has generated positive operating cash flow in just 1 of the last 5 years, and FCF has worsened every single year, reaching -INR 2,415 Cr in FY25. Reported earnings of INR 505 Cr are essentially fictional from a cash perspective.

The balance sheet deterioration in FY25 is alarming enough to be disqualifying on its own. Borrowings nearly quadrupled in 12 months — from INR 1,513 Cr to INR 5,669 Cr — while CWIP ballooned from INR 14 Cr to INR 1,322 Cr. Something large and capital-intensive is being financed with cheap debt at a moment when interest rates remain elevated; finance costs of INR 265 Cr are growing faster than revenue. The D/E ratio of 1.83 far exceeds my ceiling of 0.5. Even at a forward P/E of 7.4x, I would not buy this business — price is what you pay, value is what you get, and what you get here is a treadmill that requires ever-larger capital injections to stand still.
